frames.narration: A sorted list of 1,000 prices and a budget no pair can match. Trying every pair means 499,500 checks, and the work forgets what it learned: pair (0, 1) says nothing about pair (0, 2).

Two pointers: one at the smallest item, one at the largest. If their sum is too small, the left item cannot pair with anything, so the left pointer moves up. If too big, the right pointer moves down. Each check rules one item out for good.

messages.label: sum too small: left moves up

frames.narration: Result: 999 checks instead of 499,500. The sorted order is the reason each move is safe. On an unsorted list the same moves would skip real pairs.
A trap in the testing: if the target pair sits early in the pair order, trying every pair stops after 1,997 checks and looks fine. A test where no pair exists shows the real cost.

Now the longest run of days with total spend at most 500, over 10,000 positive amounts. The right pointer adds an amount, the left pointer drops amounts while the total is too big. Each amount enters once and leaves at most once: 19,900 steps, against 1,001,650 for trying every start.

Why it is correct: with positive numbers, a window that is over the limit stays over the limit if it grows to the right, so its start can be abandoned for good. That one sentence is the proof, and it only holds if no amount is negative.

Break it: refunds arrive, so amounts range from -3 to 5. A total can now come back down, and dropping the left item throws away a start that would have worked. With 1,000 amounts and a limit of 500 the window answers 502 in 1,499 steps. The true answer is 506.

The safe fallback, trying every start, can no longer stop early and costs 500,500 steps for the same 1,000 items. Faster correct methods exist for this data, but they are a different algorithm. The lesson: say which property of the data the fast version depends on, and test against the slow version.
